prompt: I want to turn the debugging procedure we worked out yesterday into a SKILL.md so future sessions reuse it. Can you write it?
I wrote a skill for our deploy process but Claude never seems to pick it up even when I ask about deploys. What's wrong with it?
Review the markdown files under .claude/skills/ and tell me which ones are badly written.
Our agent loop has a retry-with-backoff path and a tool-result truncation path. Write tests for both that run in CI with no API key.
The test suite for our LLM agent takes 40 seconds and randomly fails because it hits the real Anthropic API. Fix the approach.
How do I prove in a unit test that my agent really runs two tool calls concurrently instead of one after the other?
Our autonomous coding agent dies after ~60 steps with a request-too-large error from the model API. Each step appends a big file read. Fix it.
Add a max-spend-in-dollars option to the agent runner so a run stops cleanly when it crosses the cap.
Prompt caching never hits after our agent trims old messages — cache reads are zero on every request. Why, and how do we trim without losing the cache?
My Python tree-walking interpreter dies with 'maximum recursion depth exceeded' when a guest program recurses 5000 deep. How should I restructure the evaluator?
Add proper tail calls to the interpreter in interp.py so a tail-recursive loop of a million iterations runs in constant stack.
There's a sys.setrecursionlimit(100000) hack at the top of our evaluator module. Get rid of it without breaking deep programs.
Our interpreter keeps every intermediate version of a list for undo history, and appending in a loop makes memory grow quadratically. Fix the data structure.
I need a persistent (immutable) list type in plain Python where push is cheap even though old versions stay alive. No third-party libraries.
Profiling shows 67% of interpreter time is spent building display strings for values that are never printed. What's the fix?
Find bugs in the parser and evaluator under languages/whence/ — crashes, not style issues — and pin each one with a regression test.
All 200 tests are green but I don't trust that they prove much. How strong is this suite really, and how do I make it stronger?
Harden the expression evaluator in calc.py before we ship it.
Our CLI is supposed to exit 1 on a failed check and 2 on a parse error, and print errors to stderr. Nothing tests that. Add tests.
The README shows example output for every command in examples/ but nobody has verified it in months. Make that impossible to drift.
Unit tests pass but when I actually run ./tool from the shell it prints a traceback. How do I catch this class of bug automatically?
Design and implement a small scripting language in Python with a lexer, parser and evaluator, with tests.
We need a tiny config/expression DSL so users can write rules like `price > 100 and region == "EU"`. Build the evaluator.
Add string interpolation and a `while` loop to the interpreter in languages/mini/, with tests.
Build a small calculator language with a `run.py` CLI; the CLI must exit non-zero on errors and that must be tested end to end.
Random-program testing of my interpreter keeps finding RecursionError crashes on deeply nested input. Fix the root cause and keep the fuzzing loop going.

Our status page computes each outage's duration by subtracting the first failing health-check timestamp from the last one. We poll every 15 minutes, so those numbers must be low. Make the reporting honest.

The incident review says the database was unreachable for 5h14m, but the postmortem doc says 6h. Both are derived from the same monitoring log. Which one is right and how do we stop this disagreement recurring?
We want to claim last night was the longest downtime we've ever had, but we only find out a host is down when the hourly cron probe runs. Can we actually prove it beat the previous record?
Our config loader rejects bad files with `invalid key: retires` and users keep filing that as a bug. I want the messages to tell people what to write instead.
The interpreter prints `expected a list, got a function` — accurate, points at the right argument, and three people this week reported it as a defect in the library. What should change?
Someone wants to fix our CLI's confusing validation failures by expanding the README and silently auto-correcting mistyped flag names. Is there a better option?
This suite has been green for months, but it has only ever run in one working directory on one box. How do I find out whether it still passes from a fresh clone?
One of our tests builds its input corpus with glob() over a data directory and asserts there are at least 20 files in it. A separate agent also writes files into that directory. Is that a problem?
`git status` here has shown the same dozen untracked files for months and nobody remembers who wrote them, while the tests pass every day. Should I care?
Our lexer's docstring has said statements are newline-separated since its first commit, but the parser happily accepts two of them on one line. Should I make that an error, and how do I do it safely?
The README says config keys must be lowercase and the loader takes uppercase ones without complaint. I want to start rejecting them without wrecking the good error messages we already have.
Go through our spec and module docstrings for sentences using must / always / only, and tell me which of those the code does not actually check.
Write a bash script that renames all .jpeg files in a folder to .jpg.
Explain the difference between Python's asyncio.gather and asyncio.wait.
My Flask endpoint returns 500 when the JSON body is missing a field. Add validation and a 400 response.
Optimize this SQL query: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM customers WHERE region = 'EU').
Write a React component that renders a paginated table of users.
Add type hints to utils.py and make mypy pass in strict mode.
Our local llama.cpp server feels really slow on long prompts. Can you measure TTFT and tokens/sec at a few prompt sizes so we have actual numbers?
vLLM says it has prefix caching enabled but agent turns with our 8k system prompt still take forever. How do I check whether the KV cache reuse is actually working?
I need prompts of exactly 1000 and 4000 tokens for a timing test but the box only has bare python, no tokenizers package. What's the way to do this?
Write a pytest benchmark that times our JSON parser on a 10 MB file and fails if it regresses more than 20%.
Our fuzzer has reported 0 crashes for three runs now, but I'm sure the new compiled fast path in the evaluator gives different answers than the old tree-walker on some inputs. How do I find those?
I had Claude review interp.py and it listed six 'bugs'. I don't trust the list — can we make it prove each one before I open tickets?
The random-program campaign against our interpreter shows a bunch of timeouts and I've been ignoring them. Worth looking into or is that normal?

Our colibri qwen36 engine re-prefills the whole 26k-token transcript on every turn even though the server has a --kv-slots option. Can you read the serve loop and figure out whether KV state can persist across requests, and draft an upstream patch? I can't restart the box.

Turn 5 of a chat on my self-hosted C inference engine takes about five times longer than turn 1 — nothing changed except the history got longer. Identical repeated prompts aren't faster either. What's wrong in the engine and how would I fix it?

The model behind our agent is a hybrid Mamba-plus-attention thing and the serving code resets everything per request. I want to propose prefix caching upstream but I can only compile, not run the weights. How do I validate a patch like that?
Before I run the benchmark for the new caching layer I want to write down what we expect so we can't fool ourselves afterwards. Set that up properly.
Every time I optimize something I claim 2x and get 1.3x when it's re-measured. How do I stop overestimating before I measure?
We just ran the A/B on the new index and it's 'faster', but nobody agreed beforehand what would count as a win, so the result is meaningless. Fix our process so this doesn't happen again.

The previous autonomous session of this project crashed halfway through; the state notes say the mutation run is 'in progress' but I see finished JSON result files on disk. Sort out what actually happened before we continue.
I'm resuming a long-running agent job that got killed by a rate limit overnight. What should I check before I start the next step?
Load average is 12 on my laptop and the last research run finished hours ago. Also there are test files in the repo that nobody remembers writing. What's going on?
Train a time-series model to forecast next week's sales per store from the last two years of data.
Add session persistence to my Flask login so users stay logged in after the server restarts.
Write a post-mortem for yesterday's production outage: root cause, timeline, and action items.

Our box runs a 35B MoE engine that fills all 31 GB of RAM (MemAvailable is 580 MB, swap is in use). Someone wants to run a 1B model next to it as a fast lane for short tool calls. Is that feasible, and how would we even get the 7 GB weights onto the machine without evicting the big engine?

I need to copy a 7 GB model container onto a server whose inference engine is pinned at its cgroup MemoryMax. A plain scp last time pushed the engine into swap. What's the safe way to stage the file, and can I resume if the copy dies halfway?

The small second model we added beside the production LLM decodes at 2 tok/s and gets SLOWER when I give it a bigger expert cache; top shows sys time above user time. The machine has almost no free memory. What's going on and what should I measure?
We're adding a second GPU node to our Kubernetes inference cluster and want two replicas of the same model behind a load balancer. How should we configure the autoscaler and readiness probes?

Our agent runs keep ending with the model writing `read_file(path=src/x.py, start=1, end=40)` as plain text instead of an actual tool call, and the loop records the run as completed. How do we catch and recover those?
Three of our sonnet review runs came back with an empty final answer or the literal text 'tool call: search' and we paid for them anyway. Change the harness so that doesn't count as done.
Last night's kill-stage results are mostly 'failed' at steps 1-3 with nothing scoreable in the final text. Look at what the model actually replied and make the loop robust to it.
Add a JSON schema validator for our REST API's request bodies and return a 400 with per-field errors when a body is malformed.

Our agent pipeline hits a CPU inference box where a 900-token prompt takes two minutes of prefill. I want each step declared with its lane, prompt, reply cap and a time budget, and the runner should refuse a step that can't fit the remaining budget before it sends anything. Retries with backoff and a JSONL trace too.

We have a small fast model and a big slow one on the same server. Route short classification jobs to the small one and fall back to the big one when it fails, keep the whole chain under 4 minutes, and tell me afterwards which call spent the time.
The box is down until tomorrow but I need to know today whether this five-step model pipeline fits in a 10-minute window per run, given the latency numbers we already measured.
Benchmark our llama.cpp server: measure time-to-first-token and decode tokens per second at 100, 1k and 4k prompt tokens and plot the curve.
note: boundary case: the sibling skill's territory (measure the curve), not the task-script skill; round 112 probe fired llm-engine-benchmarking 3/3 and never preflight-priced-task-scripts

prompt: Our bash driver runs a while-true loop launching agent rounds forever. We just fixed a bug in the script, but the process that has been running for two days is still doing the old broken thing. Do we need to kill and restart it, or is there a way to make it pick up the fix on its own?
I want our long-running bash orchestration loop to pick up code changes automatically, without an external watchdog script that has to kill and relaunch it every time we ship a fix.
ps shows the same PID for our driver process from three days ago, but its log output still looks like the OLD format even though we edited the script yesterday. What is going on?
Our systemd service keeps restarting after every deploy. Add a health check so it only restarts when a request actually fails, instead of on every deploy.

The driver log says round 12 finished and round 13 already started, but 'ps' still shows round 12's claude process alive with an 8-minute uptime, and both are editing the same repo. Am I safe to start writing files, or could round 12 still be mid-edit?

Our cron job runs `claude -p "do the round's work" --max-turns 100` once per iteration. Three iterations in a row show the driver log marking them 'success' with 60-150 tool calls each, but no files changed and no report was written. The last line of each transcript says something like 'I'll resume once the background job finishes' or 'standing by for the notification.' What's going on and how do I stop it from happening again?

I have a non-interactive batch pipeline that invokes an LLM agent once per task. Every so often a task is marked done with no error, but nothing it was supposed to produce actually exists on disk. It looks like the agent kicked off a long-running check and then stopped issuing any more tool calls.
The overnight automated run finished clean, no errors, but this time absolutely nothing changed. The very end of the transcript just says the process is waiting for something to complete.
In my interactive Claude Code session, I want to kick off a long build in the background and keep working on something else while I wait for it to finish, then get notified when it's done.
Our interpreter has tail-call elimination. I want to prove it can't change any observable behaviour, not just that the return values match. How would you test that?
We have a test that compares the cached and uncached code paths, but it strips the timestamps and request ids out of both before diffing. That feels like cheating. Is it?

Our compiler folds constants at parse time. A user reports the error message points at a different line when folding is on. Both lines are arguably right — how do we decide which one the compiler should say?
Our architecture docs and code comments are full of references like "see ADR-014" and "per invariant I3". Nobody has ever checked that those actually exist. Can you find the ones that point nowhere?
SPEC.md has a numbered list of design decisions that stops at 13, but the parser's comments cite decision 27, 28 and 29. Where did those come from and what should we do about it?
I want to turn on a docs linter across a 200-file repo that will definitely be red on day one, and I don't own half of what it will flag. How do I roll it out so the team doesn't just delete it?
Our README links to https://example.com/docs and it 404s now. Find every external URL in the repo that's dead and update them.
Our CONTRIBUTING.md has a '## Release process' heading with nothing under it. Everyone cites 'the release process' in review comments. I guess nobody ever wrote it — can you draft one?

The code reads a config key BUILD_PROFILE that isn't defined in any of our config files or docs. Before I go ask the platform team to spec it out, is there any way to tell whether it used to be documented?

Writing up an audit finding: the coding-standards doc our lint config points at is an empty stub, and it predates our git history, so reconstructing the standards is going to need a decision from engineering leadership. Sanity-check my reasoning before I send this.
A test started failing sometime in the last two weeks and I can't tell which change did it. Help me narrow down the commit.
I lost about an hour of edits when my editor crashed — the changes were never committed. Anything I can do to get them back?

Our sprint carryover doc has re-listed the same three open items verbatim every week for two months. Before I copy it forward again, I want to know whether any of them are actually still true, and I'd like that checked automatically from now on.
The 'Known limitations' section of our README still says the importer is capped at 4096 rows. Someone raised that cap ages ago. How do I find the rest of these and stop the list drifting again?
Every weekly status update we write starts as a copy of last week's. What can go wrong with that, and how would you catch it without asking everyone to be more careful?
We have a MockPaymentGateway that was copied from the real gateway two years ago, and both are still edited by hand. How do I work out what the real one gained since that the mock never got?
Our golden-file generator emits a field layout the production serializer stopped producing three releases ago, and the whole suite is still green. Where do I start?
A subclass overrides build_report() and the override body is recognisably the parent's body with one line changed. Is that worth doing anything about?

In our schema DSL, naming a type that was never declared reports 'unknown type' when it appears in a field, but silently evaluates to null when it appears in an argument. Same user mistake, two different outcomes.
Our validator keeps declared shape names in one flat dictionary, while ordinary value bindings get proper push/pop frames. Is that asymmetry going to bite us, and what do we do about it?

There's a comment in our type checker saying the fragment table is 'deliberately not scope-aware', next to an UnboundName sentinel that exists so a lookup that 'cannot happen' stays safe. Should I trust that?

Our uptime checker reports a gap as `verified: true` whenever the surrounding log covers it, but the docstring right above it admits it can't detect a suspend. It's feeding a dashboard that says '0 minutes unverified'. Fix the claim.

This function returns a boolean 'no data loss occurred' but the only evidence it has is the first and last record in the window. I want it to say how much loss could still be hiding instead of just yes/no.
Two of our health rules rule out exactly the same failure and one is labelled STRONG and the other WEAK, and the STRONG one is why the report shows None for worst-case downtime. Sort this out.
Change this function to return True instead of 1 so mypy stops complaining about the return type.

Our differential test skips any input where the two builds are allowed to answer differently. I want to know how often that skip actually fires and whether the reason we wrote down is the reason it fires.
Adding a known-acceptable-divergence list to this comparison checker. Reviewer says just return early on those. Is there a better way to write it?

This audit reports only its failures, so a suppression that hits 5% of rows looks exactly like one that never hits anything. I inherited the suppressions and have no idea which still earn their place.
Add a # noqa: E501 to line 42 so the linter stops complaining about the long URL in that comment.

We shipped a Rust port of our Python config parser and there's a test that runs 400 real config files through both and diffs the parsed result. Green since day one. A customer just hit a file the Rust side happily loaded and the Python side has always thrown on.
Our JS and Go implementations of the same document format are supposed to behave identically. The conformance suite is 200 documents that all load fine. What am I missing from that suite?

The reference interpreter returns an error record and the production one raises, so we never compare the two on malformed input — the shapes don't line up and the text is worded differently anyway. Is there anything in there worth testing?
Rename the `errors` module to `diagnostics` throughout the package and fix up the imports.

Our incremental test runner skips a suite when the fingerprint hasn't moved. The fingerprint is a sha over every .py file under src/. In practice almost nothing is ever skipped — a one-line docstring edit in an unrelated package busts the whole thing. How should I make the fingerprint tighter without guessing wrong?

We had a bad one yesterday. A benchmark result got served as current even though someone had edited the .sql template it loads at runtime. The stamp only covers the Python sources, so the edit was invisible to it. I want to fix this properly rather than bolting *.sql onto the glob and waiting for the next surprise.

I'm adding a constant at the top of the invalidation module listing which packages actually matter to the report generator, with a comment telling people to keep it up to date when they add an import. Does that hold up, and is there a better shape for it?

I want to know which modules in our package transitively import `models.py` so I can plan a refactor. Everything is plain top-level imports, no dynamic loading. What's the cleanest way to get that graph?

I ran our repo's own consistency script by hand for the first time in months and it fails on something that was merged back in March. CONTRIBUTING says to run it before opening a PR and clearly nobody does. Before I go ask for CI budget I want to know how bad this has actually been, not just that it's bad.

Problems in our docs tree keep getting found by whoever happens to open that directory next, never by the PR that caused them. It's happened three times this quarter. Can we put a number on how long these sit before someone trips over them?
A colleague wants to add a fifth validation script to the repo. We already have four and as far as I can tell nobody has run any of them since they were written. What should I say in review?
Our CI lint job has been failing on main since this morning. It reports three flake8 errors in api/handlers.py. Fix them.

My log-scan script returned zero results after running for 1417 seconds against a 1400 second timeout, and it wrote that zero to disk as a finding. I'm about to bump the timeout to 3000. Is that the right fix?

I need to pick a batch timeout for a job that runs over ~40 partitions. A couple of them are enormous and most are tiny. Whatever number I pick is wrong for one end or the other. How should I approach this?
We have a sweep over the whole archive that can't finish in one CI run. Every time we try it we lose the work and start over. I want it to make progress across runs without redoing anything.
Our health-check endpoint has a 2 second timeout and it occasionally trips when the DB is slow. All the checks do the same single query. Should we raise it to 5 seconds?

We added a per-file cache key to the CI test cache last month and I claimed it would roughly double hit rate. I can't re-run CI a hundred times to check. Is there a way to actually measure whether it helped?

Our build-artifact staleness rule has two parts, a source hash and a dependency hash. Something is invalidating everything constantly and I can't tell which of the two is doing it. How do I find out without instrumenting a month of builds?
I want to compare our current cache-invalidation scheme against two variants we never shipped, using our real commit history rather than a synthetic benchmark. What would that look like?
Every entry in our results ledger is stamped with a hash of the source tree, but when I try to find the commit that hash came from, none of them match. Can these records be audited at all?
My unit test suite takes four seconds. I changed the cache key and want to know if it's faster now.

Our rule is that every incident gets a postmortem. I have no idea how many actually got one: the incidents are Jira tickets and the postmortems are scattered across Notion pages, a few Google Docs, and some markdown in the repo, with no naming convention. Before I ask for a bot I want to know what we're actually missing and who owes it.

Every ADR in our repo is supposed to end up with an entry in docs/decisions.md, but people often write the outcome in the PR description or a Slack thread instead and never circle back. Can I get a list I'd actually trust of which ADRs are still undecided?

A contractor handed their project to us halfway through. We merged all their branches and the tests pass, but I have a nagging feeling the open questions they raised in their design docs went nowhere. How would I check that systematically rather than by reading everything?
Our CI step that uploads coverage to Codecov has been silently failing for two weeks because the exit code is swallowed by a pipe. Fix the pipeline so it fails loudly.

Our security scanner reports the same three findings on every build. They were all triaged months ago and are waiting on a vendor fix. I want the build green, but if the vendor ships a change to one of those files I absolutely need to know. Adding them to the ignore list feels wrong.

We have a known-failures baseline file for the test suite. Half the entries are for tests that were deleted a year ago and nobody noticed, so the file reads like it covers more than it does. How should a baseline like this be structured so it can't rot?

A separate system writes into our repo and one of the files it edits is checked in. A reviewer already looked at the current edit and decided to leave it. Every audit run since then re-reports it and people have stopped reading the audit output. What's the right way to record 'we already decided this' without going blind to the next edit?
Our linter has been flagging the same unused-import warning in one module for weeks. Can you just delete the unused import?

Our coverage dashboard says '412 of 418 services checked this week' and leadership reads that as 412 healthy. The checker stores each run's pass/fail per service but the dashboard only shows the last-checked timestamp. Something feels off about the number but I can't articulate what.

Each package in our monorepo gets a status from the most recent CI run that touched it. But when a run fails we re-run just the failing packages, so a package's status usually comes from its own retry. Is the per-package status telling us what we think it is?

An audit reports every dataset as 'validated' against the current schema version. I dug in and one dataset's validation touched two of its nine tables, and another was validated four times on the same table. The audit counts validations, not tables. How should I restructure this so the summary line can't be quoted as a quality number?
Our nightly integration suite has been failing for three days on the same assertion. Can you look at the assertion and tell me whether the expected value is still right?

Our inference server's RSS has been flat at 30.8 GB for the last nine hours, so I think that's just its footprint at the cache size we configured. Can you sanity-check that before I sign off on the sizing?
We measured the process at cache_size=256 and got 36 GB, so I scaled it linearly to pick 204 for the new box. Does that math hold up?
This service has been fine in prod for months and now it OOMs maybe once a week, always under weird traffic. Nothing was deployed. Where would you start?
The per-entry size constant in our pool sizing code came straight out of the file header, but I just noticed the loader decompresses each blob before it caches it. How much does that matter?
Memory climbs about 40 MB an hour and never comes back down, with no configured cache size anywhere. Help me find the leak.
This daemon mmaps every buffer at startup and never allocates again. What's a safe container memory limit for it?

Our fuzz campaign ran 2000 seeds against the new differential checker and found zero instances of the divergence we added it for. I want to write that up as 'this class does not occur' — is that a safe conclusion?
There's an exemption branch in our comparison code that has never once fired in production. Someone on the team wants to widen it to cover a second case. How should I evaluate that?
This alert has not paged anyone in fourteen months. Can we delete it, or do we need to prove something first?
Our flaky-test detector fired on 37 of 1200 test runs last week, up from 12 the week before. Can you dig into what changed?

The design doc says we didn't fix the exporter because it would mean touching every one of the several hundred call sites of `emit()`, and because the format has no field for the tenant id. I'm about to write that up as 'not feasible this quarter'. Should I?

There's a comment in the cache layer saying re-hydrating per request 'would dominate the request time', which is why we keep this stale global. Three teams now quote that sentence. Nobody has a number for it.
Reopening a ticket that was closed as won't-do. The closing comment lists four reasons the migration is impossible. How should I work through it before I commit the team to anything?
We've never attempted the Kafka migration and there's no prior write-up. Give me a rough estimate of how long it would take.
We priced all three blockers on the deprecation last week and two are real. Given that, should we do it this quarter or next?

Our nightly job log ends with `SUITE OK (412 files scanned, 0 stale)` and that same line has been identical for two weeks. I want to write in the design doc that the job rescans everything nightly. Is that safe to state?
CI is printing `build: PASS (FAILED integration/test_billing.py::test_refund)` on the same line. The exit code is 0. What is going on and how should I fix the reporting?
I'm adding a `deploy status` subcommand that re-prints the last recorded rollout verdict from a ledger file. What should it print so nobody mistakes it for a live check?
A ticket says the ETL validates every partition on each run, and cites the pipeline summary output as evidence. Before I plan work on top of that assumption, how should I check it?
This integration test fails about one run in five with a timeout. Help me work out whether it's the test or the service.
Our log lines are hard to read in the terminal. Can you suggest a nicer column layout for the per-file status output?
Our prompt-selection eval fired the new instruction 0 times out of 3 on its own test cases. I'm going to write that into the baseline file as a known-bad prompt and move on. Sound right?
Two evaluation reports for the same model disagree about whether the summarizer regressed. The newer one is from last night, so I'm taking that one as the current answer and closing the ticket.
An integration test failed once in CI. I want to add it to the quarantine list with a note saying it's flaky so the board goes green.
We tweaked the retrieval prompt after a bad benchmark score and the second run was bad too, so I'm ready to say the approach doesn't work. Writing it up now.
Our schema linter reported three violations. It's a pure static check over the same files every time. Should I fix them or suppress them?
The latency difference between the two configs replicated cleanly across six independent runs: 240ms vs 251ms. Is an 11ms regression worth blocking the release over?

One of our tests just went red in CI with an empty diff — nobody touched the code. It builds a fake retention window from 2026-08-25 to 2026-08-31 and runs it against our live append-only audit log, and now the assertion `max_gap <= 301` is getting 15108. What happened?
This test reads state/events.jsonl, which we only ever append to, and hard-codes a covers_to timestamp in its fixture. It passes today. Should I be worried?
We have an integration test asserting `len(report['streaks']) == 2` against the production metrics store. It has been green for months. Is that assertion actually testing anything?
Audit our test suite for fixtures that pin an absolute date and are also fed real production data, and tell me which ones have quietly stopped covering what they claim to cover.
My unit test creates a tmp_path directory, writes three synthetic records dated 2026-01-01, and asserts the parser reads all three. Is hard-coding that date a problem?
Our service's RSS has been byte-identical at 30.8 GB for nine hours with no OOM, so I'm going to write that down as its footprint and size the next box from it.

Our differential oracle suite has accumulated maybe half a dozen exemption branches over the years — some skip a whole program, some drop a field, one of them is a `[:6]` slice in a loop. The campaign reports green. I want to know what it actually covers. Where do I start?

I just noticed our consistency checker only compares the first 6 items in each batch — it's a literal slice in the loop bound and nothing logs what it skipped. Before I change it, how do I find out whether there are other caps like this and how much they're costing us?

We have a suppressions file with 40 entries that nobody has audited since it was created. Some of them probably matter and some are probably dead. How would you evaluate the whole set rather than arguing about them one at a time?
I'm adding one new exemption to our comparison code — these two forms are genuinely allowed to differ when the spec name is shadowed. What's the right way to write that branch?
Our oracle suite takes 6 minutes per campaign and `determinism` is the slowest. Can you profile it and find where the time goes?

We added helpful hints to our validator's error messages last quarter and unit tests cover every one of them, but users still hit the same wall and our sample scripts exit 0 printing blank fields. Figure out what is going on.
Add a `did you mean ...?` suggestion to our interpreter's unbound-variable error, picking the closest variable name currently in scope by edit distance.

Our audit tool walks git history and tells us a rule has been violated at every commit for the last three months, still open. Nobody has ever seen it fail when they run the checker themselves. I need to know which of the two is lying before I file a bug against the whole quarter.

I want to write something that goes back through our commits and reports how long each lint rule has been broken. The linter reads a config file and a directory of generated reports, and the reports are in .gitignore. Is that going to give me an honest number?

We have a nightly job that checks the working tree and a separate script that reconstructs old revisions and checks those. They have never once flagged the same thing. My lead thinks that means we have great coverage.
How do I make `git archive` include submodules when I export a tag for release?

I want a cron sweep to commit the metrics file it writes so the next session stops inheriting it. Two worker processes both append to the same shared events.log and we intermittently get interleaved half-lines. Sometimes worker A wins, sometimes B, and the corruption shows up maybe one run in twenty. What is the right locking approach here?

A comment in our allocator says MAX_FRAMES is the real upper bound on how big a node can get, and cites the stress test that hits it. Our nightly audit prints '0 stale entries' and everyone treats it as clean. I do not think it says how many entries it looked at, and I suspect on some nights it enters no tier at all and still prints zero. How should the summary line be written so that zero means something?

Our doc checker just flagged eleven expected-output claims across the repo as stale. Every one of them says a smaller number than the suite actually prints now. I'm about to go through and update each one to the current count — anything I should do differently?

Our event log rows have a `precision` column that says whether the timestamp was measured or reconstructed from a rounded uptime string, and I just noticed none of our analytics queries look at it. They all just compare timestamps directly. How much should I care?

We have one function that decides both 'this proves the service was down the whole time' and 'this proves someone reached it mid-outage', and both branches use the same `<=` against a sampled timestamp. That feels wrong but I can't articulate why.

Our nightly quality report runs eight linters plus a `make check` target and builds one table by grepping each command's stdout for error codes. Is my grep wrong?

The status page for our test pipeline shows a coverage percentage for every job. The integration-suite job and the smoke-suite job have printed byte-identical coverage figures for months, and the integration suite is the one that shells out to run the smoke suite. Where should I look first?

I built a script that attributes each red CI check to whichever tool reported it, by parsing the aggregate log. The wrapper job that invokes all the other tools comes out as the top reporter of every category, which cannot be right, and its own failures only ever say 'exit 1' with no detail. How do I make that row say something true?
Write a Python function that parses a pytest -q summary line like '3 failed, 120 passed in 12.34s' into a dict of counts.

Our dependency scanner prints 'unresolved: 131 call sites' at the end of every run and the number has been in the README for months. The next ticket says to widen the resolver until that count comes down. Before I do that, is there anything I should check about the 131 itself?

A coverage tool we wrote reports a 'skipped' bucket that it says it cannot analyse statically. I want to quote that bucket as our known blind spot in a design doc. How do I make sure the bucket really is what it claims to be?

One predicate in our AST walker decides both whether a call executes code and whether its first argument is a source string, and the walker's 'could not determine' list keeps growing. Should I add an ignore list for the call sites that keep showing up in it?
Our CI job intermittently reports a different number of collected tests between runs on the same commit. How do I make pytest collection deterministic?

Our ADR index in docs/adr/README.md lists ADRs 1 through 31, but somebody merged a PR last month that added docs/adr/0032-event-bus.md without touching the index. I was about to open ADR 32 for a different topic. How do I stop this happening again?

Our docs linter says `error code E014 is referenced in 6 places but is not in the error-code table`. I can just add the row, but I have a nagging feeling the linter only catches this when something happens to reference the code. Is there a better check?

Every RFC in our repo is written twice: a one-line summary in the RFC index with `(v2.4, sprint 61)` after it, and the full document under rfcs/. Nothing checks that the version and sprint in the index match the ones in the document header. Worth building, or am I inventing work?

Our SOC2 evidence tracker stores, per control, the log file path plus the exact log line that proves the control fired. A nightly job greps the line out of the file and marks the control green. We have a docs test that asserts each code snippet in our tutorials also appears verbatim in the example repo. It caught a real drift once.
